statements.claim: Kamsa lay dead with his brothers, and the men of Mathura stood stunned among the fallen while the wives of the slain warriors wept and lamented over their husbands on the field.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.44.41-48: the women, grieving at the slaying of their friends/husbands, lament over the husbands lying on the heroes' bed (v.42-43 'teṣāṃ striyo... śayānān vīra-śayāyāṃ patīn āliṅgya śocatīḥ'); Kamsa's death and his brothers' fall are the immediately preceding canonical events (DKS_0141, Bhagavata 10.44.36-40).

statements.claim: The widows called to the dead by tender epithets — lord, beloved, knower of righteousness, kind to the shelterless — and mourned the city left without its protector.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.44.44-45: 'hā nātha priya dharma-jña karuṇānātha-vatsala / tvayā virahitā patyā purīyaṃ puruṣarṣabha'.

statements.claim: Even Kamsa's wives wept, and the sound reached the palace and the streets.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87: Ugrasena hears 'the heart-rending lamentations of Kansa's wives' bewailing their husbands; pack excerpt (SB 10.44.41-48) covers the royal women's weeping.

statements.claim: Krishna did not turn away; he walked among the royal women, comforted them, and had the customary funeral rites prepared for the dead.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Bhagavata 10.44.41-48, confidence 5): 'Krishna comforted the royal women and had the customary funeral rites performed for the dead'.

statements.claim: Ugrasena, burning with grief and breathing like a man who had drunk poison, came and reproached himself in the assembly of the Yadavas for having made widows of these thousand women.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (1-4): 'Breathing like a person who has drunk poison, Ugrasena, burning with grief for his son, approached Krishna... censuring his own self in that assembly of the Yādavas... I have... made widows of these thousand women.'

statements.claim: Ugrasena reflected that Kamsa was sinful, hated by the pious and ruthless of temper, so that death was better than such a life, and that the wicked reap their fruits by death while the pious reach auspicious ones.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (7-12): 'Death is preferable to life unto him who... is of a degraded conduct, ruthless temper... Kansa was highly sinful, never liked by the pious... Those, who are wicked, are constrained by Death to reap the proper fruits. The pious attain to auspicious fruits.'

statements.claim: Ugrasena asked leave to perform Kamsa's after-death rites — to build the pyre, put fire to it and offer the water-oblation — after which he would range in the forest with his wife and daughters-in-law.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (26-30): 'Having performed the after-death ceremonies of that king... I shall, along with my wife and daughters-in-law, range in the forest with the animals... having made his funeral pyre, putting fire to it and offering oblation of water I shall have discharged debt to Kansa... This is my only prayer.'

statements.claim: Krishna was filled with surprise at Ugrasena's words and answered with consolation: what Ugrasena said befitted his age, family and nature; the inevitable work being done, Kamsa would still receive funeral honors befitting a king, and destiny is inevitable.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (31-34): 'Hearing the words of Ugrasena, Krishna was filled with surprise. And consoling him he said: ...what you have said behoves your age and family... Although dead, Kansa will receive funeral honors befitting a king... Why do you not then understand that destiny is inevitable?'

statements.claim: Kamsa's body was placed in a palanquin and carried to the northern bank of the Yamuna, where the pyre was raised, fire set, and the obsequial rites performed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (58-59) excerpt: 'desirous of performing the obsequial rites of king Kansa according to the ritualastic laws they placed his body in a palanquin and took it to the northern bank of Yamuna... setting fire to the pyre.'

statements.claim: The day that began with the wrestling match ended with the funeral, and Mathura had to bury its dead before enjoying its freedom.
statements.evidence: Framing close to the story; the corpus treats the lament and rites as the same aftermath event (evt_0146); the Harivamsha has the cremation on the following morning, but the pack's own Bhagavata-based summary presents the rites within this episode, so no contradiction is asserted.

notes: Faithful to Bhagavata 10.44.41-48 and Harivamsha 1.87; the long Ugrasena/Krishna exchange maps verse by verse to the pack's Dutt translation.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama walked into the prison where Vasudeva and Devaki were still bound, released them from their bonds themselves, and bowed to touch their parents' feet.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.44.49-50: 'mātaraṃ pitaraṃ caiva mocayitvātha bandhanāt'; pack excerpt: 'Krishna and Balarama released Vasudeva and Devaki from their bonds and bowed, touching their feet'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva and Devaki, knowing their sons to be the lords of the world, embraced them without fear.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.44.50: 'devakī vasudevaś ca vijñāya jagad-īśvarau' ('knowing [them to be] the lords of the world'); pack excerpt: 'the parents, knowing their sons to be the lords of the world, embraced them without fear'.

statements.claim: Kamsa killed Devaki's children one by one as they were born, and the last two sons were smuggled out of the prison on the night of their birth — Krishna carried across the Yamuna by his father, Balarama taken to safety before him.
statements.evidence: Canonical arc background established in earlier corpus events (the six slain children and the night transfers of Balarama and Krishna, per Bhagavata 10.2-10.3 and prior stories); consistent with this pack, uncontradicted.

statements.claim: For eighteen years those gates had held Vasudeva and Devaki, and the cell had been a cage for nearly two decades.
statements.evidence: No support in the pack (Bhagavata 10.44.49-50 / Vishnu Purana 5.20) or anywhere in the corpus chain. The corpus only establishes that Krishna dwelt in Vraja for eleven years (DKS_0016, SB-based) and that the imprisonment began before the children's births; the total duration is nowhere quantified, so the specific figure 'eighteen years'/'nearly two decades' is unsupported.

statements.claim: She had been told, on the night Krishna was born, that her eighth child would be the death of Kamsa.
statements.evidence: The corpus's own canonical event (DKS_0003, Bhagavata 10.1.28-33, Vishnu Purana 5.1, Harivamsha 1.56) places the eighth-child prophecy at Vasudeva and Devaki's WEDDING, when Kamsa drove the chariot and heard the bodiless voice — years before Krishna's birth. The story shifts the prophecy to Krishna's birth night, which contradicts the established account.

statements.claim: The parents remembered the words Krishna spoke at his birth, when the chains fell from their hands and he promised to return when the time came, and the promise had been kept.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.20 (pack): Vasudeva and Devaki bowed to Krishna, 'recalling to recollection what he had said to them at his birth'; consistent with the birth-night release of the chains in the earlier corpus chain.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama had grown up in Gokula knowing their parents only as names, and came to their parents before the throne, the city, or anything else victory might have claimed.
statements.evidence: Framing of the reunion (Vraja upbringing is canonical chain background); the ordering against the throne/city is the story's reflective framing, not a sourceable assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: For eighteen years those gates had held Vasudeva and Devaki — the couple whose children Kamsa had feared so much that he killed them one by one, and whose last two sons had been smuggled out of that very prison on the night of their birth.
corrections.suggested: All the years of Kamsa's reign those gates had held Vasudeva and Devaki — the couple whose children Kamsa had feared so much that he killed them one by one, and whose last two sons had been smuggled out of that very prison on the night of their birth.

corrections.original_sentence: She had been told, on the night Krishna was born, that her eighth child would be the death of Kamsa, and she had watched Kamsa take her children from her, one after another, as they were born.
corrections.suggested: She had been told, on the night of her wedding, that her eighth child would be the death of Kamsa, and she had watched Kamsa take her children from her, one after another, as they were born.

corrections.original_sentence: Every fear she had carried for eighteen years had been about these two young men who now knelt at her feet.
corrections.suggested: Every fear she had carried through all the years of her imprisonment had been about these two young men who now knelt at her feet.

corrections.original_sentence: The chains lay on the floor of the cell, and the room that had been a cage for nearly two decades had become, in the space of a few breaths, the place where a family stood whole.
corrections.suggested: The chains lay on the floor of the cell, and the room that had been a cage for so many years had become, in the space of a few breaths, the place where a family stood whole.

notes: Core reunion is faithful (SB 10.44.49-50 + VP 5.20). Two issues: (1) 'eighteen years'/'nearly two decades' duration is unsupported anywhere in the pack or corpus (corpus only gives 11 years in Vraja, DKS_0016); (2) the prophecy is misdated to Krishna's birth night — the corpus canon (DKS_0003) has the voice at the wedding procession.

statements.claim: Krishna, who had broken the great bow, felled the wrestlers and ended Kamsa, stood bowed before his parents asking their pardon, with Balarama at his side.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.1: 'uvāca pitarāv etya sāgrajaḥ sātvanarṣabhaḥ' (the best of the Satvatas, with his elder brother, approaching the parents, spoke); bow/wrestlers/Kamsa are the established preceding events of the arc.

statements.claim: Krishna told his parents they had ever longed for them, but struck by fate they could not dwell near them, though the parents wished it with all their hearts.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.2-3: 'nāsmatto yuvayos tāta nityotkaṇṭhitayor api / na labdho daiva-hatayor vāso nau bhavad-antike'.

statements.claim: Krishna said the body that becomes the seat of every purpose is born and nourished from the parents, and the debt owed to a mother, father, aged parent, devoted wife and young son no one can repay with himself or all his wealth.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.4-6: 'sarvārtha-sambhavo deho janitaḥ poṣito yataḥ / ... mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vṛddhaṃ bhāryāṃ sādhvīṃ sutam śiśum'; v.5 'ātmanā ca dhanena ca'.

statements.claim: He confessed that kept from them by Kamsa, their minds never at peace, they could not serve their parents as sons should, and asked forgiveness — 'we were in the power of another'.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.7-8: 'tan nāv akalpayoḥ kaṃsān nityam udvigna-cetasoḥ / tat kṣantum arhathas tāta mātar nau para-tantrayoḥ'.

statements.claim: Vasudeva and Devaki could not answer at first; they reached out and held their sons, their tears fell on the sons' heads, and the old rope of affection bound the four of them together.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.10 (given in the following episode's passage): 'siñcantāv aśru-dhārābhiḥ sneha-pāśena cāvṛtau' (the two, pouring streams of tears, bound by the rope of affection); parents' tears and embrace are the pack's depicted response.

statements.claim: The two parents had been helpless for eighteen years in the prison.
statements.evidence: Specific duration appears in no source: this pack covers Bhagavata 10.45.1-9 only, and the corpus nowhere quantifies the imprisonment (cf. DKS_0143 note); the corpus only establishes eleven years in Vraja (DKS_0016) plus unquantified pre-birth years.

statements.claim: There was no anger or settling of accounts in the prison that day; the sons who had been taken came back asking forgiveness rather than giving it, and asked only that their parents forgive them for the childhood they had missed.
statements.evidence: Reflective commentary on the plea; consistent with the pack's account of the humble request for forgiveness, no new factual assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: He had just taken back from Kamsa everything Kamsa had stolen — the city, the throne, the years — and the first thing he did with it was kneel before two people who had been helpless for eighteen years and ask their forgiveness for a childhood he had never been allowed to give them.
corrections.suggested: He had just taken back from Kamsa everything Kamsa had stolen — the city, the throne, the years — and the first thing he did with it was kneel before two people who had been helpless in their bonds for all those years and ask their forgiveness for a childhood he had never been allowed to give them.

notes: The apology speech is a faithful rendering of Bhagavata 10.45.1-8, nearly line by line. Single issue: the 'eighteen years' duration (echoed from DKS_0143) is unsupported by the pack or corpus.

statements.claim: Ugrasena, Kamsa's father, had been set aside and confined by his own son, who took the throne and ruled; Krishna later released his grandfather from confinement.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.21 (pack): 'The foe of Madhu then liberated Ugrasena from confinement, and placed him on the throne, which the death of his son had left vacant'; Kamsa's usurpation is canonical arc background (corpus chain, uncontradicted).

statements.claim: Krishna did not take the throne himself; before the assembled Yadavas he declared Ugrasena would be king, saying that because of Yayati's curse no Yadava was to sit on the throne.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (Bhagavata 10.45.11-13, confidence 5): Krishna 'installed his maternal grandfather Ugrasena as king of the Yadavas, declaring that because of Yayati's curse no Yadava should sit on the throne'; Harivamsha 1.87 (55): installation 'in that assembly of the Yadus'.

statements.claim: Ugrasena protested that he cared nothing for the kingdom or the royal throne and told Krishna to take it for himself and win glory by becoming king.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (48-52, Dutt): it is KRISHNA who says 'I do not care for the kingdom or the royal throne. I did not slay Kansa for a territory... I stand in no need of the kingdom', and Krishna who instructs Ugrasena: 'place yourself on the throne and acquire victory by becoming the king'. Ugrasena had offered Krishna Kamsa's army, wealth and lordship (22-24) and spoke of retiring to the forest (26-28); he did not protest that he cared nothing for the kingdom. The story swaps the speakers.

statements.claim: Krishna, knowing the law, was not moved, and Govinda, well read in the laws, installed his grandfather on the throne that his son's death had left vacant.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (52-55): 'place yourself on the throne and acquire victory by becoming the king... Then Govinda, well read in laws, installed him on the throne'; Vishnu Purana 5.21: 'placed him on the throne, which the death of his son had left vacant'.

statements.claim: Krishna had said that while he served at his grandfather's side, the very gods themselves would pay tribute to the throne.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.13: 'mayi bhṛtya upāsīne bhavato vibudhādayaḥ' (while I serve as your attendant, the gods and others [shall honor] you).

statements.claim: He did not take the crown, the wealth or the army; he gave them to the man Kamsa had wronged, and the king was the man Kamsa had tried to erase.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.87 (48-53): Krishna declines Kamsa's army and wealth ('I do not care for the kingdom... I stand in no need of the kingdom') and abdicates the kingdom to Ugrasena; VP 5.21 installation.

statements.claim: The boy from Gokula, who had arrived in Mathura that morning as a stranger and left it the master of everything, stood at the foot of the throne and placed an old man upon it.
statements.evidence: Rhetorical compression of the two-day arc (arrival, arena, coronation); 'that morning' is loose (corpus chain has them reach Mathura the previous day, DKS_0131) but functions as connective summary, not a core factual assertion.

corrections.original_sentence: He protested that he cared nothing for the kingdom or the royal throne, and told Krishna to take it for himself and win glory by becoming king.
corrections.suggested: He spoke of performing the rites and retiring to the forest with his wife and daughters-in-law, and pressed Kamsa's kingdom and wealth upon Krishna; but Krishna refused, saying he cared nothing for the kingdom or the royal throne, and instructed his grandfather to place himself on the throne and win glory by becoming king.

notes: Installation and Yayati's-curse rationale are supported (SB 10.45.11-13 excerpt; VP 5.21; HV 1.87). One contradiction: the refusal scene is role-swapped — in Harivamsha 1.87 (48-52) Krishna says he does not care for the kingdom and tells UGRASENA to take the throne, while the story puts that protest in Ugrasena's mouth.

statements.claim: The Yadava, Vrishni, Andhaka and Madhu kinsmen had fled in fear of Kamsa to every direction, and Krishna brought them all back and settled them again.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.14: 'sarvān svān jñāti-sambandhān digbhyaḥ kaṃsa-bhayākulān'; pack excerpt: 'Krishna brought back all the Yadava, Vrishni, Andhaka and Madhu kinsmen who had fled in fear of Kamsa, settled them in their homes with wealth'.

statements.claim: Krishna honored each returning kinsman, comforted them in their exhaustion from dwelling abroad, and restored their wealth.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.15: 'sabhājitān samāśvāsya videśāvāsa-karśitān' (honoring them, comforting those wasted by foreign residence); pack excerpt: 'settled them in their homes with wealth'.

statements.claim: Protected by the arms of Krishna and Balarama, they obtained everything their hearts had desired for years.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.16: 'kṛṣṇa-saṅkarṣaṇa-bhujair guptā labdha-manorathāḥ' (protected by the arms of Krishna and Sankarshana, they obtained their heart's desires).

statements.claim: Day after day the rejoined clans gathered to look at Krishna's face, and the sight of him was delight enough; even the oldest became young again, vigorous as youths.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.17-18: 'vīkṣanto 'har ahaḥ prītā mukunda-vadanāmbujam / tatra pravayaso 'py āsan yuvāno 'ti-balaujasaḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna sent word to every corner of the earth for the exiles to come home, and they returned by twos and threes, dusty from long roads, some so long gone their grandchildren had never seen Mathura.
statements.evidence: The return from all directions is v.14 ('digbhyaḥ'); the mechanism ('sent word'), the dusty arrivals and the grandchildren are connective elaboration consistent with the exile (videśāvāsa-karśitān, v.15), not separately sourceable.

statements.claim: Weddings that had been postponed for a decade were held at last.
statements.evidence: No support in the pack (Bhagavata 10.45.14-18) or in any other corpus evidence: the verses celebrate daily gazing on Krishna's face (v.17) and restored youth (v.18) but never mention weddings or a decade of postponement.

statements.claim: When the last exile was settled in his father's house, Mathura was whole again, the clans one under one king, since before Kamsa seized the throne.
statements.evidence: Summarizing connective close consistent with v.14-18; no new unsupported event asserted beyond the restoration already covered.

corrections.original_sentence: Weddings that had been postponed for a decade were held at last.
corrections.suggested: And the rejoicing that the years of exile had deferred broke out at last in every courtyard.

notes: Close to Bhagavata 10.45.14-18, including the striking v.18 detail of the aged becoming young. One unsupported invented flourish: weddings 'postponed for a decade' being held — the verses speak only of daily rejoicing at Mukunda's face.

statements.claim: Vasudeva summoned the brahmins and had the sacred-thread ceremony performed for Krishna and Balarama, who received the initiation and became twice-born students.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.25, 28: 'atha śūra-suto rājan putrayoḥ samakārayat... labdha-saṃskārau dvijatvaṃ prāpya su-vratau'.

statements.claim: For the officiating brahmins Vasudeva gave a fee of cows adorned with golden necklaces, richly decorated — the very cattle he had mentally pledged at the ceremonies following the births of his two sons.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.26-27: 'tebhyo 'dād dakṣiṇā gāvo rukma-mālāḥ sv-alaṅkṛtāḥ / yāḥ kṛṣṇa-rāma-janmarkṣe mano-dattā mahā-matiḥ'.

statements.claim: The two who stood before the brahmins were already the lords of all knowledge, all-knowing, masters of the world, yet they desired to live in a guru's house like any students.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.29-30: 'prabhavau sarva-vidyānāṃ sarva-jñau jagad-īśvarau / atho guru-kule vāsam icchantāv upajagmatuḥ'.

statements.claim: They went as students to the teacher Sandipani in the city of Avanti, served humbly with blameless conduct, and pleased the brahmin teacher by their pure dispositions.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.30-32: 'guru-kule vāsam icchantāv upajagmatuḥ / yathopasādya tau dāntau gurau vṛttim aninditām / tayor dvija-varas tuṣṭaḥ śuddha-bhāvānuvṛttibhiḥ'; pack excerpt: 'went to the teacher Sandipani in Avanti'.

statements.claim: Sandipani taught them the science of the bow with all its secret doctrines, the codes of duty, and the paths of justice and reasoning.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.33: 'sa-rahasyaṃ dhanur-vedaṃ dharmān nyāya-pathāṃs tathā'.

statements.claim: In sixty-four days and nights the brothers mastered all the arts and sciences Sandipani could teach.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.45.34-35: 'sarvaṃ... sarva-vidyā-pravartakau / aho-rātraiś catuḥ-ṣaṣṭyā saṃyattau tāvatīḥ kalāḥ' ('in sixty-four days and nights attained all those arts').

statements.claim: When the sixty-four days were done the brothers were finished students ready to take their leave, and the teacher's fee had not yet been spoken of.
statements.evidence: Close of the episode consistent with v.33-35; the fee request follows immediately in the canon (Bhagavata 10.45.36ff, next corpus event) — connective transition, uncontradicted.

notes: Faithful to Bhagavata 10.45.25-35 nearly verse by verse (initiation, the mentally-pledged cows, 64 days-and-nights, the guru's syllabus).

statements.claim: Knowing the longing of the love-tormented Sairandhri (Trivakra, the woman whose crooked back he had straightened), Krishna went to her house, taking Uddhava with him.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.1-3: her house 'rich with splendid furnishings' seen as he approached; 'tathoddhavaḥ' present; pack excerpt: 'Knowing the desire of the love-tormented Sairandhri, the Lord went to her house'. The earlier straightening is canonical chain (VP 5.20 passage, pack of DKS_0143).

statements.claim: When she saw him approaching, she rose at once, flustered; Uddhava, honored for his goodness, sat on the ground, touching the seat that was offered, leaving the place of honor for his lord.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.2-3: 'sadyaḥ samutthāya hi jāta-sambhramā / tathoddhavaḥ sādhutayābhipūjito nyaṣīdad urvyām abhimṛśya cāsanam'.

statements.claim: She prepared herself with bath, fragrant unguents, silk and ornaments, garlands and perfumes, betel and sweet drinks, and drew Krishna near by his bangle-adorned hand, shy at the newness of his nearness.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.4-5: 'sā majjanālepa-dukūla-bhūṣaṇa-srag-gandha-tāmbūla-sudhāsavādibhiḥ... āhūya kāntāṃ nava-saṅgama-hriyā viśaṅkitāṃ kaṅkaṇa-bhūṣite kare'.

statements.claim: She embraced him, pressing him to her breast with both arms, and in that embrace her long torment ended, for she held the blissful form before her.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.6: '...parirabhya kāntam ānanda-mūrtim ajahād ati-dīrgha-tāpam' (embracing the beloved, the very form of bliss, she gave up her exceedingly long torment).

statements.claim: She had obtained what the whole world calls hard to obtain — the lord of liberation himself standing in her small house.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.7: 'saivaṃ kaivalya-nāthaṃ taṃ prāpya duṣprāpyam īśvaram' (she obtained the lord of liberation, the lord hard to obtain).

statements.claim: She asked only that he stay with her a few days — not wealth, power, or a place in his court.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.8: 'sahoṣyatām iha preṣṭha dināni katicin mayā' (dwell here with me, dear, for a few days); the 'only' framing is a fair reading of the single request recorded.

statements.claim: Krishna, who honors those who honor him, granted her the boon she wished, and when he left he returned to his own abode.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.9: 'tasyai kāma-varaṃ dattvā mānayitvā ca māna-daḥ'; pack excerpt: 'Krishna granted her the boon she wished and returned to his own abode'.

statements.claim: Her home was rich and furnished with splendid things, arranged with care for the one she hoped would come.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.48.1: 'mahārhopaskarair āḍhyaṃ kāmopāyopabṛṃhitam' (rich with splendid furnishings, furnished with love's means).

notes: A close rendering of Bhagavata 10.48.1-10: each beat (rise in fluster, Uddhava taking the ground, the toilette list, the embrace that ends her long torment, the 'few days' request, the granted boon) maps to a verse.

statements.claim: Sudama, Krishna's old classmate from the guru's house, came to Dwaraka, and Krishna asked whether he remembered their days in the guru's house.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.30: 'kaccid guru-kule vāsaṃ brahman smarasi nau yataḥ' (do you remember, brahmin, our dwelling in the guru's house); Sudama's arrival in Dwaraka is the canonical frame of SB 10.80 and the corpus's Sudama arc (DKS_0287-0289).

statements.claim: Krishna said the guru's house is the true birth of a twice-born and the direct root of all good deeds, and that he is not reached by sacrifice, sons, austerity, or a merely quieted mind — but by such days as those spent at a teacher's feet.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.31-33: 'sa vai sat-karmaṇāṃ sākṣād dvijāter iha sambhavaḥ... nāham ijyā-prajātibhyāṃ tapasopaśamena vā'.

statements.claim: Sent by the guru's wife to gather firewood, the two boys entered the great forest; the sun had set, darkness covered every direction, and a violent wind and rain struck them again and again in the rising water.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.35-37: 'praviṣṭānāṃ mahāraṇyam... sūryaś cāstam gatas tāvat tamasā cāvṛtā diśaḥ / vayaṃ bhṛśaṃ tatra mahānilāmbubhir nihanyamānā muhur ambu-samplave'; pack excerpt: 'sent by the guru's wife to gather firewood'.

statements.claim: Lost in the blackness, they held each other's hands and wandered until at sunrise the guru Sandipani, who had known where they were, came through the storm to find them.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.38: 'etad viditvā udite ravau sāndīpanir guruḥ'; pack excerpt: 'lost in the darkness and holding hands, they wandered till the guru found them at sunrise and blessed them'.

statements.claim: The guru said: 'Ah, my sons, you have suffered so much for my sake. This is exactly what true disciples must do — this is the repayment of the guru. I am pleased with you. May your wishes come true.'
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.39-41: 'aho he putrakā yūyam asmad-arthe 'ti-duḥkhitāḥ / etad eva hi sac-chiṣyaiḥ kartavyaṃ guru-niṣkṛtam / tuṣṭo 'haṃ... satyāḥ santu manorathāḥ'.

statements.claim: Krishna closed the memory: 'Such were the days we spent in the guru's house. There were many like that one.'
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.80.42: 'itthaṃ-vidhāny anekāni vasatāṃ guru-veśmani' (many such days there were, living in the guru's house).

statements.claim: The two sat in silence — the lord of Dwaraka and the brahmin from the south, both boys again in the dark forest — and the memory showed what the years under Sandipani had made of them.
statements.evidence: Closing atmosphere; Sudama's being a brahmin is the text (v.27 'brahman', v.41 'dvija-śreṣṭhāḥ'); 'from the south' is an unverified descriptor of his village (the pack's 10.80.27-42 range does not state it) and 'the years under Sandipani' compresses the shared gurukula days — connective, no contradiction.

notes: The recollection maps directly onto Bhagavata 10.80.30-42, including the guru's blessing at sunrise nearly word for word (v.39-41). The storm-and-darkness night (v.36-37) and the 'many such days' close (v.42) are exact.
